title: byte-granularity-spill-model-proposal
content:
Purpose:
This note proposes an alternative spillback model for the KV cache that works at fine-grained byte/segment granularity instead of the current page/block unit. The goal is to reduce unnecessary paging I/O and memory bandwidth spikes in workloads with very skewed token reuse (long-tail keys and partial-key reuse across requests). This doc records rationale, microbench design, early measurements, and an initial rollout plan.

Summary of idea:
- Current behavior: eviction & spill operate on fixed-size pages (4KB/2MB depending on allocator), which is simple but can cause large read/write amplification when hot items partially overlap pages.
- Proposed: split large entries into small immutable segments (configurable, default 64B/256B) stored contiguously but indexed at segment granularity. Eviction and spill decisions operate on segments with heuristics to coalesce adjacent cold segments lazily.
- Expected benefits: lower read amplification on partial hot-key accesses; smoother memory bandwidth usage; better aligned eviction to token reuse patterns for transformer KV streams.
- Tradeoffs: larger metadata overhead (segment index), increased CPU for bookkeeping, potential fragmentation that must be mitigated with periodic coalescing.

Definitions and metrics to evaluate:
- segment_size: bytes per atomic spill unit (experiment with 64, 256, 1024).
- reuse_rate(segment): fraction of lookups hitting the same segment within reuse_window (example formula: hits(segment,last_N_accesses)/N).
- effective_bandwidth(Bw_eff): measured DRAM bandwidth attributable to KV operations (profile counters per-host).
- spill_write_amp: bytes written to SSD/NVMe per logical bytes evicted.
- read_amp: bytes read from storage to satisfy misses per logical tokens served.
- tail_latency_99: 99th percentile request latency.

Microbenchmark design (local lab VM cluster):
- Workloads: three synthetic traces built from real production token traces (anonymized):
  1) prefix-heavy: large proportion of requests reuse initial KV prefixes (simulates chat single-turn reuse).
  2) interleaved-subkeys: many requests access different subranges of the same large context (simulates tool-calls + documents).
  3) long-tail-sparse: Zipfian key popularity with alpha=1.4, lots of cold keys.
- Config matrix: segment_size in {64,256,1024}, total_cache_small/med/large, background_coalesce {on,off}, prefetch_hinting {none,aggressive}.
- Measurement collection: perf counters for memory bandwidth, kernel iostat for NVMe BW, runtime histograms for latency and per-seqlen KV misses, and a small tracer to sample per-request segments touched.

Early results (single P4d-like node emulation):
- prefix-heavy: segment_size=64B -> 18% drop in read_amp vs 4KB pages, tail_latency_99 improved ~7ms on median requests; CPU overhead +6% due to index lookups.
- interleaved-subkeys: 256B segments gave best tradeoff, read_amp -22%, spill_write_amp reduced 35% (fewer whole-page writes), but fragmentation grew ~12% over baseline after 24h synthetic run (we measured free pool fragmentation).
- long-tail-sparse: gains smaller (~5-8% bandwidth) because misses dominate; metadata overhead became noticeable for smallest segment size (64B) and increased GC pressure.
- memory bandwidth smoothing: segment-based spill reduced instantaneous bandwidth spikes (measured burst BW at 50 ms windows) by ~30% in interleaved workload.

Observability notes:
- We added two counters to the agent prototype: segments_evicted, segments_coalesced, and segment_index_entries. These were critical to correlate fragmentation with write amplification.
- Added a sampling trace that records up to 5000 segment ids touched per minute to estimate reuse_rate distribution. Useful to detect when coalescing should be aggressive.

Implementation sketch (runtime changes):
1) segmentation layer: when a new large KV chunk is inserted, split into immutable segments. Keep a small header mapping logical offset->segment ids (compact representation).
2) segment index: lock-free hash table mapping (model_id, sequence_id, segment_offset) -> segment metadata (last_access_ts, resident_flag, storage_loc). Use compact 48-bit tags to reduce memory.
3) eviction policy: operate on segments; score = recency_decay*age + size_penalty + (estimated_bandwidth_cost for reread). Prefer spilling segments with low reuse_rate and high resident size.
4) coalescer: background task that merges adjacent cold segments into larger units for storage efficiency during low load. Trigger heuristics: low CPU usage, low BW, contiguous segments with similar cold score.

Rollout plan (canary -> progressive):
- Stage 0: feature-flagged on a single-serving-pool in staging; segment_size=256, coalescer=off. Run synthetic interleaved-subkeys trace for 48h.
- Stage 1: internal canary on low-percent of traffic (2%) in prod-like fleet; enable sampling counters; monitor tail_latency_99, read_amp, spill_write_amp, memory fragmentation (free pool).
- Stage 2: if metrics stable (<3% CPU regress, read_amp improvement >= 10%), enable coalescer in a separate canary and observe storage write patterns for 7 days.

Open questions / risks:
- Metadata size growth: smallest segment sizes make index larger than the data in worst cases. Need accurate cost model to choose default.
- SSD endurance: smaller writes increase write amplification unless coalescer keeps up. We must benchmark with realistic SSD geometry.
- GC/compaction CPU: coalescing must be throttled to avoid interfering with inference. How to backpressure?
- Cross-node migration: Dedicated pools with shared migrations will need an efficient way to transfer segment maps; naive transfer is expensive. Consider checkpointed coalesced images for migration.
- Interaction with prefix/KV caching: current prefix caching assumes contiguous context blocks; segmentation changes the assumption. Need to ensure prefix cache still benefits.

Short experiments to run next (ordered):
- Run a 1-week long mixed workload (real anonymized traffic) with segment_size {256,512} and measure SSD write amplification.
- Measure CPU overhead per 1M requests at production p99 QPS using profiler to find hotspots in index lookup code-path.
- Run a hardware NVMe endurance model to estimate additional TBW consumed at scale for segment sizes 64/256/1024.
- Prototype a light-weight Bloom filter per logical key to avoid full index lookups on cold misses (reduce extra CPU for 64B segments).

Decision criteria for default config:
- Choose smallest segment_size where: read_amp reduction >= 12% and CPU overhead <= 5% and SSD write_amp increase <= 10% vs baseline. Early numbers suggest 256B is promising.

Notes to reviewers (what I want feedback on):
- Are we comfortable with introducing per-segment metadata in the hot path? Suggestions for compressing metadata?
- Thoughts on coalescer triggers (time-based vs BW-based)? Should coalescing be prioritized by SSD write queue depth?
- Any known interactions with Dedicated cluster migration code I should be aware of?

Appendix: lightweight config example (pseudo-toml)

[kv_spill]
segment_size = 256                  # bytes
coalescer = true
coalesce_idle_seconds = 120        # only run when host CPU < 20% for this long
index_reserve = 0.08               # fraction of cache for metadata index in worst case
eviction_score = "recency*0.7 + (1/estimated_reuse)*0.3 + write_cost"

End of note.
